subject: Dedicated capacity sizing & pricing — Nimbus Health (GPU pool recommendation)
messages:
From: Samir Khan <samir.khan@nimbushealth.com>
To: vanessa_ortiz <vanessa_ortiz@redwood.com>
Cc: contracts@nimbushealth.com
Date: 2026-03-02T09:15:00-07:00
Subject: Initial sizing data and a couple questions

Vanessa — thanks again for the demo this morning. As discussed, here are the rough production metrics we promised so you could recommend Dedicated sizing and pricing: 

- Baseline average request volume: 12 requests/sec (across 3 microservices)
- Peak (95th pctl) burst: 48 requests/sec for 10–20 minute windows
- Typical concurrency per model: 40 active sessions; spikes to ~120 concurrent streams during certain workflows
- Median context length: 2.2k tokens; 90th percentile: 7.5k tokens
- Average tokens per response: 420
- Model family: Llama-2 style 70B (we're evaluating quantized variants)

Questions from our infra/procurement side: what committed reserve do you recommend (GPU count and commit hours) to meet throughput/SLOs, and what discount tiers are possible for a 12 vs 24 month commit? Also need an estimate for 99th-percentile latency tail at the recommended configuration.

Samir
Director of AI Platforms
Nimbus Health

Subject: Re: Initial sizing data and a couple questions

Samir — thanks for the detail, this is perfect. Looping in Sean (solutions / performance) and Priyom (pricing & commercial). We’ll do a quick pass with sizing assumptions and give a conservative proposal plus a lower-cost optimized option.

Quick clarifying Qs before we run numbers:
- Are all three microservices hitting the same model instance, or do you shard models across services?
- Expected growth rate over the next 12 months (sustained QPS growth)?
- Any hard latency SLOs for 99th percentile (e.g., <350ms token/warm-start, <1.5s end-to-end)?

I’ll start with a baseline recommendation and a 2-tier pricing/commitment schedule.

—Vanessa
Account Exec, Redwood Inference
From: sean_gallagher <sean_gallagher@redwood.com>
To: vanessa_ortiz <vanessa_ortiz@redwood.com>, Samir Khan <samir.khan@nimbushealth.com>
Cc: priyom_das <priyom_das@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-03-03T08:24:00-07:00
Subject: Proposed GPU pool & perf assumptions (first pass)

Samir — I ran a quick perf projection based on the metrics you shared and our internal benchmarks for 70B-family quantized at int8. Highlights / assumptions: 

- Sustained throughput target: 15 req/s (gives buffer over your 12 req/s baseline and accounts for growth)
- Burst target: support 45–48 req/s for 15 minutes without dropping connections
- Tail latency target: 99th token latency ~ 250–350ms on warm path; end-to-end 99th percentile (first token) ~ 1.2–1.7s depending on batch size
- Model memory: quantized 70B uses ~40–60GB effective memory with KV cache pressure for 7–8k contexts

GPU pool recommendation (conservative / production-safe):
- 3 x A100-80GB-class workers dedicated (24/7 reserved) to handle sustained traffic and KV cache residency for 7–8k context lengths
- 1 x hot-burst node (same family) in burst pool to absorb short 95th-percentile spikes; automatic routing during peak policy
- Autoscale headroom for brief spikes via our burst pool (adds up to 50% short-term capacity)

Why this mix: the 3 reserved GPUs ensure KV cache fits the working set and maintain predictable latency; the extra burst node prevents queuing during peak windows while keeping committed cost lower. If you’re willing to accept higher quantization (int4) and slightly higher tail latency, a cost-optimized configuration drops to 2 x A100 reserved + 1 burst node.

I’ll hand off to Priyom for the commercial with monthly committed hours and discount options.

—Sean
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
From: priyom_das <priyom_das@redwood.com>
To: Samir Khan <samir.khan@nimbushealth.com>, vanessa_ortiz <vanessa_ortiz@redwood.com>
Cc: lauren_bishop <lauren_bishop@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-03-03T11:40:00-07:00
Subject: Pricing & commit options for the recommended pool

Samir — following Sean’s recommendation, here are two concrete commercial options (all $ amounts illustrative; final quote in attached PDF):

Option A (Production-safe, preferred):
- Reserved: 3 x A100-80GB equivalent GPUs, 24/7 reservation (720 hours/mo per GPU -> 2160 GPU-hours/mo total)
- Burst: 1 x hot node available for short spikes (pay-as-you-burst at a discounted ad-hoc rate)
- 12-month commit: 15% discount off list dedicated rate; monthly billable: $48,000/mo (net after discount)
- 24-month commit: 20% discount; monthly billable: $43,200/mo (net)
- Add-on: Optional 2-week warm cache pre-provisioning for cutover: one-time $6,000
- SLA: 99.9% uptime on dedicated pool, latency SLOs agreed in annex

Option B (Cost-optimized):
- Reserved: 2 x A100-80GB equivalent GPUs, 24/7 reservation (1440 GPU-hours/mo total)
- Burst: 2 x hot nodes available for up to 1 hour / day (to handle spikes)
- 12-month commit: 10% discount; monthly billable: $31,500/mo (net after discount)
- 24-month commit: 14% discount; monthly billable: $28,000/mo (net)

Notes on pricing mechanics and flexibility:
- We can structure commits as monthly or annual billing; discounts scale with contract length and total committed GPU-hours.
- For true elasticity during onboarding, we recommend Option A for the first 60 days, then evaluate telemetry for right-sizing (we’ll include Optimize suggestions).
- If Nimbus has procurement constraints around multi-year obligations, we can propose a hybrid: 12-month guaranteed + 12-month optional renewal with price caps.

I attached a worksheet that maps expected QPS/context-length to required GPU-hours; that’s the source for the commit numbers. Happy to walk through line-by-line on a call.

—Priyom
Principal Pricing Manager, Redwood Inference
From: Samir Khan <samir.khan@nimbushealth.com>
To: priyom_das <priyom_das@redwood.com>, vanessa_ortiz <vanessa_ortiz@redwood.com>
Cc: laura.cheng <laura.cheng@nimbushealth.com>, contracts@nimbushealth.com
Date: 2026-03-04T10:07:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Pricing & commit options for the recommended pool

Thanks, team — this is very helpful. A few follow-ups from procurement and infra: 

1) Can you publish the expected 99th-percentile P95/P99 token latencies for Option A vs Option B under our actual traffic mix (I’ll attach the sample traffic CSV).
2) Is the burst node billed only when active? Any cold-start penalties for routing to burst nodes?
3) For the 24-month commit numbers, can you include an explicit termination/cap adjustment schedule (procurement wants exit terms spelled out)?

We’re leaning toward Option A but want a clear ramp plan and a bridge for month-to-month in case our usage grows faster than predicted. Also cc’ing Laura from procurement to coordinate PO cadence.

Samir
From: lauren_bishop <lauren_bishop@redwood.com>
To: Samir Khan <samir.khan@nimbushealth.com>, priyom_das <priyom_das@redwood.com>, vanessa_ortiz <vanessa_ortiz@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-03-05T09:33:00-07:00
Subject: Follow-up: answers & next steps

Samir — quick answers inline and next steps: 

- Latency numbers: we’ll produce a small perf matrix (P50/P95/P99 token latencies) for Option A and B using your attached CSV and our synthetic replay. Expect P99 token latency delta of ~70–150ms between A and B at 7–8k contexts; end-to-end P99 should still be within your 1.7s requirement on Option A. We’ll post the exact table by EOD tomorrow.
- Burst billing: burst nodes are metered only while active; you only pay the discounted burst-hours used. There is a short warm-up (few hundred ms for cold tokens) if the routing decision brings a new node out of standby, but our routing policy prefers warm workers for high-percentile requests.
- Termination/adjustment: we can include a 90-day ramp-down schedule for GPU-hours with a staggered credit back (standard enterprise playbook). I’ll send legal-friendly language for procurement to review.

Next steps: attach the sample perf matrix and the revised PDF proposal with the termination language. Can we set a 30-minute sync for Wednesday (3/10) to go over final numbers and procurement asks?

—Lauren
Director, Solutions Operations, Redwood Inference
